proposed_front_matter.title: Multi-ciphertext security degradation for lattices
proposed_front_matter.venue: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, Report 2022/1580 (preprint; received 2022-11-14, revised 2023-03-17)
proposed_front_matter.citation_verified_basis: Full 55-page PDF retrieved 2026-08-05 from https://cr.yp.to/papers/lprrr-20230317.pdf (HTTP 200, 821460 bytes, sha256 7b0e27261f4f9abcd7aa02fc9e3ed441b1f2d5b2ae3d7b5352f47e325e04f970) and read; version and bibliographic details cross-checked against the live ePrint landing page for 2022/1580 (HTTP 200, same date). The ePrint PDF endpoint itself returned 403.

proposed_body_sections.Contribution: Quantifies, under the existing lattice-attack heuristics, how the security of typical lattice PKEs/KEMs degrades when one public key carries many ciphertexts. Three analyses: (section 2) single-target asymptotics and parameter optimisation; (section 3) an attack breaking MANY ciphertexts for one key at total heuristic cost asymptotically equal to a single-target attack, not relying on key recovery; (section 4) an attack breaking ONE OUT OF many ciphertexts, beating single-target message recovery by 2^{Theta(n / lg n)}. Appendix A identifies gaps in the prior literature's arguments for multi-target safety, including a proof-gap analysis of Duman-Hoevelmanns-Kiltz-Lyubashevsky-Seiler (ACM CCS 2021). Appendix B gives a 2^88-guess attack breaking one out of 2^40 ciphertexts for a FrodoKEM-640 public key.
Key claims (as reported): If parameters give the usual single-target message-recovery attack heuristic cost 2^{(1+o(1))L}, then total heuristic cost 2^{(1+o(1))L} decrypts T ciphertexts for any T <= 2^{(0.19...+o(1))L}; heuristic per-ciphertext cost as low as 2^{(0.80...+o(1))L}. (section 3)

One-out-of-T: the block size beta can be reduced by Theta(n / lg n) provided lg T is Theta(n). Worked example with chi = binomial on {-16..16} and Q0 = 0.501: beta drops by (0.60537... + o(1)) beta / lg beta for breaking one out of 2^{(0.0574+o(1)) beta} ciphertexts, a larger gain than the 'dimensions for free' improvements. (section 4)

Mechanism: reduce beta until single-target success probability is at least 1/T, exploiting the tail of the 2-norm distribution of the ciphertext randomness (b,d). Section 4.2 computes that distribution by generating functions (g = sum_i chi_i z^{i^2}; saddle point rho g'(rho) = y g(rho)); section 4.3 defines SqueezedLPR, an LPR variant that rejects until the squared 2-norm hits a target value, replacing s^2 by y and reducing beta by ((2 lg s - lg y)/(Q0 + 1/2) + o(1)) beta / lg beta; section 4.4 observes that an ordinary LPR ciphertext has a computable chance of being a SqueezedLPR ciphertext.

Section 4.5 constants for other error distributions (Q0 = 0.501, S0 = 0, batch at most 2^{(0.057+o(1)) beta}), computed by the Sage script in Fig. 4.5.1: binomial{-16..16} 0.60537...; binomial{-8..8} 0.59739...; binomial{-3..3}, a Kyber distribution, 0.56984...; binomial{-2..2}, another Kyber distribution, 0.54668...; uniform{-1,0,1} 0.32860....
Countermeasures named: narrower error distributions, fixed-weight ternary vectors, forcing a narrow 2-norm range at encryption, larger Q0, or modelling the variation and enlarging parameters.

Appendix A.4: the ACM CCS 2021 claim Adv^{IND-CPA} approx Adv^{(n,q_C)-IND-CPA} for lattice schemes is conditional on unlimited-sample MLWE hardness; the supporting argument is a proof outline with three steps the paper says are not justified there, one of which is exactly the many-ciphertexts-per-single-key case; and many-sample MLWE for the Kyber error distribution is already broken by Arora-Ge at a feasible sample count, which the paper says makes a proof resting on it vacuous in that range. Flaws disclosed privately 2022-11-04 and publicly 2022-11-14; no response recorded as of 2023-03-17.
Appendix B: a 2^88-guess attack breaking one out of 2^40 ciphertexts for a FrodoKEM-640 public key, against FrodoKEM's claim of a large margin.
Scope and caveats stated BY THE PAPER (d: Section 1.3: the results are asymptotic and heuristic. 'Perhaps Kyber-512 is too small for the heuristic multi-target speedups to be applicable.'

Section 1.3: sections 2-4 say that two ideas -- that the existing heuristics predict lattice security accurately, and that multi-target security matches single-target security -- CANNOT BOTH BE CORRECT. The paper explicitly does not say which is wrong: 'it seems more likely that there are serious inaccuracies in both ideas.'
Section 1.3: free-RAM model; these attacks could be outperformed by lower-memory approaches in a realistic model of computation.

Footnote 19: 'A full analysis of Kyber would also have to account for the rounding in Kyber ciphertexts ... The concrete question -- NOT ADDRESSED BY THIS PAPER'S ASYMPTOTICS; see Section 1.3 -- is then the extent to which security is damaged by variations in the effective size of (b,d).' There is no ML-KEM bit figure anywhere in the paper. The only concrete number is the FrodoKEM-640 one, which is FrodoKEM-640 and must not be transported to ML-KEM.
The attack is ciphertext/message recovery under a reused public key. It is not key recovery, and the paper stresses that hardening key generation does not protect the ciphertexts.
proposed_body_sections.Relevance to this program: This is the published dominator for the mechanism GOAL-MLKEM-005 studies: best-of-M ciphertext selection against a shared reduced basis. It claims the mechanism and its asymptotics first and more strongly, and it supplies the leading constant for Kyber's own error distributions. It also contains the program's principal counter-argument to the one-out-of-many-target IND-CPA claim of Duman et al. (CCS 2021), which is the paper any multi-target lattice proposal must clear. Cite it for the mechanism and the asymptotics; do NOT cite it for a concrete ML-KEM number, which it explicitly declines to give.
proposed_body_sections.Not verified here: The full text was read but nothing in it was re-derived, re-implemented, or experimentally checked. The Sage script of Fig. 4.5.1 was NOT run. The heuristics the analysis assumes are the standard lattice heuristics, whose accuracy the paper itself declines to endorse. Appendix A.4's characterisation of ePrint 2021/1351 could not be checked against 2021/1351 itself, whose PDF returned 403 to this environment on 2026-08-05; that verification is OPEN. Whether the CCS 2021 authors responded after 2023-03-17 was not checked.

root_cause_note.statement: The handoff's diagnosis -- that the citation_verified flag failing is the root cause of the memory-citation problem -- is consistent with what I measured, with one refinement. The flag did not fail in isolation. For KN-LIT-4974 the flag says `read` while the body says nothing was read, AND every identifier field is null, AND the tags and Relevance text describe a different subject. Any one of those alone would leave the entry findable: correct identifiers would make the exact-lookup path work even with a bad summary, and correct tags would make the keyword path work even with null identifiers. All three failed together, and the flag then asserted the result was trustworthy. 5,582 entries carry `read` with every identifier null.
root_cause_note.not_asserted: I do not assert that this is why any particular candidate generator cited Bernstein from memory. I did not observe those sessions. What is measured is that the corpus does not answer 'multi-target', 'one-out-of-many', or '2022/1580' with this entry.
